sources.title: Human History Map civilization index
sources.note: Exact id, imported label, 1492 to 1500 interval, circa flag, and other modern Métis labels assigned to the same atlas slice.

sources.title: Human History Map research coverage ledger
sources.note: Exact missing card status, state default, observed interval, border count, and unreviewed identity, chronology, and border fields.

sources.title: Human History Map missing-card queue
sources.note: Confirms the exact card is missing and identifies the imported encyclopedia source lead that is replaced here.

sources.title: Human History Map imported summaries
sources.note: Exposes a later fur-trade and voyageur summary wrongly attached to the 1492 to 1500 layer.

sources.title: Human History Map 1400 borders
sources.note: Decoded pre-appearance control for representative owners before the anachronistic feature.

sources.title: Human History Map 1492 borders
sources.note: Decoded exact polygon, positions, bounds, point memberships, overlaps, direct arcs, properties, and source feature index.

sources.title: Human History Map 1500 borders
sources.note: Decoded endpoint control showing removal of the exact feature and return to broad subsistence labels.

sources.title: Human History Map 1530 borders
sources.note: Decoded later control showing a new set of historically named layers without validating the 1492 feature.

sources.title: Human History Map Cree card
sources.note: Existing overlapping card audited and rejected as a substitute because it has a distinct identity, source scope, interval, and geometry.

sources.title: Human History Map Dënéndeh card
sources.note: Existing overlapping homeland card audited to keep distinct Dene histories separate from this atlas correction.

sources.title: Human History Map Anishinaabe card
sources.note: Existing overlapping card audited and rejected as a shared destination for the much larger imported polygon.

sources.title: Human History Map Assiniboine card
sources.note: Existing overlapping card audited to prevent its nation-specific history from being generalized across the target.

sources.title: Human History Map Blackfoot card
sources.note: Related regional card audited to prevent atlas overlap from becoming an identity or territorial claim.

sources.title: Human History Map researched overrides
sources.note: Confirms no exact override exists and records the distinct associations of already researched neighboring cards.

sources.title: Métis National Council chronology
sources.note: Métis Nation source placing emergence as a distinct Indigenous people and Nation in the late eighteenth century.

sources.title: Métis National Council language
sources.note: Métis Nation source describing Michif as its own language, developed by the early 1800s, with distinct regional varieties.

sources.title: History of The Forks
sources.note: Parks Canada overview of long Indigenous use, gathering, provisioning, exchange, and the later sequence of fur trade and settlement at the river junction.

sources.title: Land use in the precontact period at The Forks
sources.note: Parks Canada account of six millennia of meeting, fishing, seasonal camping, river travel, and far-reaching exchange at the Red and Assiniboine confluence.

sources.title: Métis National Council culture and heritage
sources.note: Métis Nation account of eighteenth-century ethnogenesis through later families and distinct communities, not a 1492 origin.

sources.title: Wanuskewin Heritage Park on Canada’s tentative list
sources.note: Parks Canada summary of a 6,400-year gathering landscape with habitation sites, bison jumps, tipi rings, a medicine wheel, and ongoing Indigenous meaning.

sources.title: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump
sources.note: UNESCO synthesis of almost six millennia of communal bison hunting, drive lanes, kill deposits, butchering camps, knowledge, and social organization.

sources.title: Prehistory of northern Saskatchewan
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan overview of limited boreal archaeology, preservation problems, plant foods, and the danger of overconfident cultural assignments.

sources.title: Prehistory of southern Saskatchewan
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan overview of material culture, late precontact bows, pottery, communal bison hunting, and evidence limits.

sources.title: Artifacts of The Forks National Historic Site
sources.note: Parks Canada collection page on Woodland projectile points, animal use, and the limits and dates of recovered objects.

sources.title: Archaeological Survey of Alberta: sites and discoveries
sources.note: Provincial archaeology volume documenting multi-component camps, bison pounds, pottery, workshops, and much later Métis wintering sites as distinct contexts.

sources.title: Laidlaw Aboriginal antelope trap
sources.note: Alberta historic register description of drive lanes, an enclosure, stone circles, and a rare communal pronghorn hunting site.

sources.title: Late precontact sites at Little Manitou Lake
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan archaeology on dated hearths, domestic and ceremonial places, changing lake conditions, and local landscape use.

sources.title: The Tschetter late prehistoric bison kill
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan record of a pound, bone bed, charcoal, and refuse pits used to interpret a specific northern Plains hunt.

sources.title: Precontact use of Saskatchewan sandhill environments
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan research on bison use, sheltered camps, firewood, plant-recovery bias, and late precontact settlement choices.

sources.title: Late precontact stone circle sites
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan research on stone circles as common northern Plains habitation traces and the limits of household reconstruction.

sources.title: Indigenous connections at Grasslands National Park
sources.note: Parks Canada overview of seasonal use by distinct nations, bison relationships, and more than 20,000 tipi rings.

sources.title: Dog sledding and pre-horse transport
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan account of dogs carrying packs, pulling plains travois and forest sleds, and horses arriving much later.

sources.title: Indigenous agriculture and plant management on the northern Plains
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan account of precontact cultivation, gathering, medicinal plants, and agricultural exchange without reducing Plains economies to one food.

sources.title: Engaged palaeoethnobotany on the northern Plains
sources.note: Peer-reviewed call for medicinal plant archaeology led with Indigenous Knowledge Keepers and Healers, noting how sparse current evidence remains.

sources.title: Traditional cultivation by northwestern Indigenous peoples
sources.note: University of Saskatchewan account emphasizing Indigenous women’s knowledge of plants as foods, materials, medicines, spiritual relations, and actively tended resources.

sources.title: Ethnobotany of Saskatchewan Woods Cree
sources.note: Later community-informed research on named plants for healing, food, craft, diapers, toys, and other uses, included only as a non-retrojective comparison.

sources.title: Precontact health evidence in southern Manitoba
sources.note: University of Manitoba research on skeletal evidence and the strict limits of reconstructing disease and care where written records are absent.

sources.title: Ethical conduct pertaining to Indigenous peoples
sources.note: Canadian Archaeological Association principles requiring community roles, consultation, respectful interpretation, and protocols for human remains and associated objects.

sources.title: First Nations learning from generation to generation
sources.note: First Nations Education Steering Committee teaching resource on family, community, Elders, stories, practice, land, and locally distinct responsibilities.

sources.title: Métis Foundational Knowledge Themes
sources.note: Métis education institute framework centering Métis voices, history, identity, language, culture, homeland, and governance.

sources.title: Family structures in Métis history
sources.note: Gabriel Dumont Institute resource distinguishing early mixed families from the later development of cohesive Métis family and community life.

sources.title: Michif language tools
sources.note: Gabriel Dumont Institute language resources explaining oral transmission, spelling variation, dictionaries, recordings, and language expert contributions.

sources.title: Heritage Michif greetings
sources.note: Gabriel Dumont Institute resource giving the modern teaching form Taanshi for hello and other Heritage Michif phrases.

sources.title: Writing-on-Stone or Áísínai’pi
sources.note: Parks Canada description of sacred Blackfoot rock art created over millennia and why pictures are not a securely dated 1492 alphabetic transcript.

sources.title: Northern Plains moccasins
sources.note: Canadian Museum of History account of early one-piece soft-soled footwear, hide materials, quill decoration, and later horse-era changes.

sources.title: Old Man’s Playing Ground
sources.note: Canadian Museum of History summary joining Piikáni oral traditions, historic sources, floodplain study, a campsite, games, and trade.

sources.title: Tse’K’wa National Historic Site
sources.note: Parks Canada and Dane-zaa stewardship account of layered archaeology, enduring oral histories, and the limits of a site far older than the target interval.

sources.title: Lower Kananaskis River archaeological sites
sources.note: Provincial inventory of campsites, fire-broken rock, butchered bone, tools, workshops, and repeated occupations near a river corridor.

sources.title: The Forks management statement
sources.note: Parks Canada recognition of thriving precontact Indigenous cultures and The Forks as the much later birthplace and heart of the Métis Nation Homeland.

sources.title: About the Métis Nation
sources.note: Métis National Council explanation of eighteenth-century fur-trade families, distinct communities, nationhood, homeland, governance, and continuing life.

proposedOverrides.name: Michif Piyii (Métis)
proposedOverrides.summary: An atlas correction separating diverse Indigenous life in 1492 from the later emergence of the Métis Nation and Michif.
